# Question

The student's data contain several variables measured for each player in each
observed season. The main question is whether the covariance of the player
effects is adequately described by a diagonal matrix, or whether it contains
a lower-dimensional factor structure.

I compare five Bayesian models:

$$
K\in\{0,1,2,3,4\}.
$$

The model with $K=0$ is the diagonal baseline. A model with $K>0$ has $K$
latent factors for the player effects. All models were fitted with Stan.

# Models

Let $y_{ij}\in\mathbb R^p$ be the vector of measurements for player $i$ in
season $j$. The model is

$$
y_{ij}=a_i+b_j+\varepsilon_{ij},
$$

where $a_i$ is the player effect, $b_j$ is the season effect, and
$\varepsilon_{ij}$ is the error. The season effects and errors have diagonal
covariance matrices in every fitted model:

$$
b_j\sim N_p(0,\Psi_b),
\qquad
\varepsilon_{ij}\sim N_p(0,\Psi_e),
$$

where

$$
\Psi_b=\operatorname{diag}(\sigma_{b,1}^2,\ldots,\sigma_{b,p}^2),
\qquad
\Psi_e=\operatorname{diag}(\sigma_{e,1}^2,\ldots,\sigma_{e,p}^2).
$$

The models differ only in the covariance of the player effects. For the
diagonal baseline,

$$
M_0:\qquad
a_i\sim N_p(0,D_a),
\qquad
D_a=\operatorname{diag}(\sigma_{a,1}^2,\ldots,\sigma_{a,p}^2).
$$

Therefore, $K=0$ means that the player covariance is fully diagonal.

For a model with $K>0$ factors,

$$
M_K:\qquad
a_i=\Lambda f_i+u_i,
\qquad
f_i\sim N_K(0,I_K),
\qquad
u_i\sim N_p(0,\Psi_a),
\qquad
\Psi_a=\operatorname{diag}(\psi_{a,1}^2,\ldots,\psi_{a,p}^2).
$$

The covariance of the player effects is

$$
\Sigma_a=\Lambda\Lambda^\top+\Psi_a.
$$

The matrix $\Lambda\Lambda^\top$ describes the covariance explained by the
common factors. The diagonal matrix $\Psi_a$ describes variable-specific
player variation that is not explained by those factors.

The scale priors have the same specification in every fitted model:

$$
\sigma_{a,k},\psi_{a,k},\sigma_{b,k},\sigma_{e,k}\sim t_3^+(0,1),
\qquad
k\in\{1,\ldots,p\}.
$$

The parameter $\sigma_{a,k}$ is used in $M_0$, and $\psi_{a,k}$ is used in
$M_K$ when $K>0$. The Stan code identifies the orientation of the factors by
using a lower-triangular loading matrix with positive diagonal entries:

$$
\lambda_{kh}=0 \quad \text{if } k<h,
\qquad
\lambda_{hh}>0 \quad \text{for } h\in\{1,\ldots,K\}.
$$

The loading priors are

$$
\lambda_{hh}\sim N^+(0,1),
\qquad
\lambda_{kh}\sim N(0,1),
\qquad
h\in\{1,\ldots,K\},\quad k\in\{h+1,\ldots,p\}.
$$

Initialization follows the working strategy in `lowrank_diag.R`: estimate
rough season means, estimate season-adjusted player means, use PCA to start
the loadings, start factor scores from those loadings, and start the remaining
scales from the variation not explained by the starting values. The existing
`lowrank_diag.R` file was not modified.

# Methodology used to choose rank

Rank selection is based on masking player-variable combinations. The unit
assigned to a fold is a pair $(i,k)$, where $i$ identifies a player and $k$
identifies a variable. If a pair is assigned to the fold currently being
evaluated, that variable is omitted for that player in every observed season.

For example, suppose $(i,k)=(17,4)$ is assigned to fold 1. If player 17 was
observed in seasons 1, 3, 4, and 6, the fold-1 fit does not see that player's
four values for variable 4. It must reconstruct those four values.

The folds are not constructed by omitting exactly one variable at a time.
Assignments are generated independently for each variable. Consequently,
several variables for player 17 may also be assigned to fold 1 and omitted in
the same fit. Variables for player 17 that are assigned to the other fold
remain available. With $p=12$ variables and two folds, the expected number of
variables omitted for a given player in either fold is $12/2=6$, although the
actual number varies by player and fold.

The construction assigns every player-variable combination to one fold:

$$
80\text{ players}\times12\text{ variables}
=960\text{ player-variable combinations}.
$$

The combinations are assigned to two folds as follows. For each variable
$k\in\{1,\ldots,p\}$, I randomly permute the 80 players. In the simulation,
the first 40 players in that random permutation are assigned to fold 1 and the
remaining 40 are assigned to fold 2. The random permutation is generated
separately for each variable. Thus, each fold contains exactly

$$
40\text{ players}\times12\text{ variables}
=480\text{ player-variable combinations}.
$$

A pair $(i,k)$ usually corresponds to several observed values because player
$i$ may be observed in several seasons.

For $m\in\{1,2\}$, define the set of individual values left out in fold $m$:

$$
\mathcal H_m
=
\left\{
(i,j,k):
\text{player }i\text{ is observed in season }j
\text{ and }(i,k)\text{ is assigned to fold }m
\right\}.
$$

When fitting fold $m$, every value indexed by $\mathcal H_m$ is omitted and
every other observed value is retained. In particular, all variables for
player $i$ whose pairs $(i,k)$ were assigned to fold $m$ are omitted
simultaneously. The two sets are disjoint, and their union contains every
observed player-season-variable value. Each observed value is therefore left
out exactly once.

The number of individual values reconstructed is larger than 960 because a
player-variable combination usually covers several seasons. Depending on the
simulated dataset, the procedure reconstructs between 4,188 and 4,584
individual values.

The main score is held-out expected log predictive density (ELPD). Cross-
validated predictive densities are a standard method for Bayesian model
comparison; see [Vehtari and Lampinen
(2002)](https://doi.org/10.1162/08997660260293292). Cross-validation has also
been used specifically to select the number of common factors; see [Toyoda
(1986)](https://doi.org/10.5926/jjep1953.34.3_252).

For candidate rank $K$ and fold $m$, let $\mathcal D_{-m}$ denote the data
retained after the values in $\mathcal H_m$ have been omitted. For
$(i,j,k)\in\mathcal H_m$, the omitted value is $y_{ijk}$. Conditional on the
model parameters and latent effects,

$$
y_{ijk}\mid\theta_{K,m}
\sim
N\!\left(a_{i,k}+b_{j,k},\sigma_{e,k}^2\right).
$$

Here $\theta_{K,m}$ collects the parameters and latent effects in model $K$.
The posterior predictive density of the omitted value is

$$
p_K(y_{ijk}\mid\mathcal D_{-m})
=
\int
p_K(y_{ijk}\mid\theta_{K,m})
p_K(\theta_{K,m}\mid\mathcal D_{-m})
\,d\theta_{K,m}.
$$

Suppose
$\theta_{K,m}^{(s)}$, with $s\in\{1,\ldots,S\}$, are posterior draws retained
from Stan. I approximate this density by

$$
\widehat p_K(y_{ijk}\mid\mathcal D_{-m})
=
\frac{1}{S}
\sum_{s=1}^S
p_K(y_{ijk}\mid\theta_{K,m}^{(s)}).
$$

The held-out ELPD score is the sum of the log posterior predictive densities
of the omitted individual values:

$$
\widehat{\operatorname{ELPD}}_K
=
\sum_{m=1}^2
\sum_{(i,j,k)\in\mathcal H_m}
\log
\widehat p_K(y_{ijk}\mid\mathcal D_{-m}).
$$

Larger ELPD is better. The score evaluates reconstruction of individual
left-out values under the simultaneous masking scheme above. It should not
be interpreted as performance when exactly one variable is missing and all
other $p-1$ variables for that player are retained. It does not treat all
seasons for one player-variable combination as one joint multivariate
prediction.

The selected rank is the value of $K$ with the largest held-out ELPD.

# Simulation study

The student's data are not currently available. I therefore checked the
procedure in simulations where the correct factor rank is known.

For each simulated dataset:

1. Generate an unbalanced panel with 80 players, 6 possible seasons, and 12
   variables. Each player appears in 3 to 6 seasons.
2. Generate player effects, season effects, and errors from the model above.
   Standardize each variable.
3. Repeat this under four different truths: $K\in\{0,1,2,3\}$. The $K=0$
   truth is the fully diagonal player-covariance case.
4. Fit all five candidate models, $K\in\{0,1,2,3,4\}$, with Stan.
5. Check whether maximum held-out ELPD selects the correct rank.

The longer run used two independently simulated datasets for each true rank,
two groups of left-out player-variable combinations, four chains, 500 warmup
iterations, and 500 sampling iterations per chain.

Maximum held-out ELPD selected the correct generating rank in all eight
simulated datasets:

\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{rrr}
\toprule
True player rank & Number of simulated datasets & Rank selected by maximum ELPD \\
\midrule
0 (diagonal) & 2 & $K=0$ in 2/2 \\
1 & 2 & $K=1$ in 2/2 \\
2 & 2 & $K=2$ in 2/2 \\
3 & 2 & $K=3$ in 2/2 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

The mean held-out ELPD per reconstructed value was:

\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{rrrrrr}
\toprule
True player rank & Fitted $K=0$ & Fitted $K=1$ & Fitted $K=2$ & Fitted $K=3$ & Fitted $K=4$ \\
\midrule
0 (diagonal) & \textbf{-1.385} & -1.390 & -1.397 & -1.402 & -1.406 \\
1 & -1.415 & \textbf{-1.021} & -1.027 & -1.030 & -1.033 \\
2 & -1.409 & -1.189 & \textbf{-0.993} & -1.002 & -1.006 \\
3 & -1.413 & -1.283 & -1.178 & \textbf{-1.060} & -1.066 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

# Two supplementary comparisons

I also ran two smaller supplementary comparisons to show that the most useful
way to leave out data depends on the intended use of the model. This
distinction matters in latent-variable models; see [Merkle, Furr, and
Rabe-Hesketh (2019)](https://doi.org/10.1007/s11336-019-09679-0).

1. Missing season: leave out all 12 variables from one observed
   player-season row. Other seasons for that player remain in the fit.
2. New player: leave out all observations for one player.

The entries below are total held-out ELPD, calculated jointly for each
left-out row or player. Larger is better.

| Truth | Supplementary comparison | Left-out units | Fitted $K=0$ | Fitted $K=1$ | Fitted $K=2$ | Fitted $K=3$ | Fitted $K=4$ |
|---:|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 0 | Missing season | 358 rows | **-5625.5** | -5630.6 | -5630.8 | -5639.6 | -5646.0 |
| 0 | New player | 80 players | -5742.3 | **-5739.2** | -5760.6 | -5774.2 | -5788.1 |
| 2 | Missing season | 354 rows | -3712.4 | -3523.2 | -3397.6 | **-3386.8** | -3410.5 |
| 2 | New player | 80 players | -6308.7 | -5139.5 | **-3942.5** | -4039.9 | -4017.8 |

The selected rank changes slightly with the supplementary comparison. For
diagonal truth, new-player ELPD is slightly larger for $K=1$ than for $K=0$.
For rank-two truth, new-player prediction selects $K=2$, while missing-season
prediction selects $K=3$. These comparisons answer different questions from
the main masked player-variable comparison.
